Ethanol: Intoxication and Safe Disposition

What Matters in the ED

  • Check glucose in altered mental status.
  • Look for trauma, infection, co-ingestion, hypothermia, occult head injury.
  • Clinical sobriety and safe discharge plan matter more than a specific ethanol level.
  • Give thiamine when malnourished, chronic heavy alcohol use, or Wernicke risk.

Wernicke Risk

Confusion + ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus + ataxia is classic but often incomplete. Treat with thiamine before or with glucose when risk is present.

Alcohol Withdrawal: Timeline, CIWA, Benzodiazepines

Table 185-1. Alcohol Withdrawal Continuum

Timeline สำคัญมาก: minor symptoms 6-24 h, seizures 6-48 h, hallucinosis often within 48 h, DT usually later and can last days.

Table 185-2 and 185-3. Withdrawal Treatment + CIWA-Ar

Benzodiazepines are first-line. CIWA-Ar helps symptom-triggered therapy in cooperative patients, but severe delirium/ICU patients need clinician-driven sedation and monitoring.

Board pearl Withdrawal seizure is usually generalized tonic-clonic; focal seizure, prolonged AMS, or trauma signs require broader neurologic workup.

Isopropanol: Ketosis Without Acidosis

Pattern

Isopropanol -> acetone. It causes CNS depression and hemorrhagic gastritis, with ketosis but no high anion gap metabolic acidosis. If severe acidosis is present, look for shock, co-ingestion, or another diagnosis.

Labs

Osmolar gap may be high. Serum/urine ketones positive. Acetone rises as isopropanol is metabolized.

Treatment

Supportive care. Fomepizole generally not indicated because acetone is less toxic than parent compound.

Toxic Alcohol Diagnosis: Gap Changes Over Time

Tintinalli source check

Table 185-5 and Figure 185-7. Osmolar Gap vs Anion Gap

Early after ingestion: parent alcohol raises osmolar gap. Later: metabolites produce anion gap metabolic acidosis. A normal osmolar gap late does not exclude toxic alcohol.

Start Treatment Before Level If Needed

If suspected methanol/EG with coma, acidosis, visual symptoms, renal failure, oxalate crystals, or unexplained osmolar gap, do not wait for send-out levels. Start metabolic blockade and call poison center/nephrology early.

Methanol vs Ethylene Glycol

Tintinalli source check

Table 185-4. Features of Methanol and Ethylene Glycol Toxicity and Treatment

Table นี้เป็นหัวใจของ chapter: sources, timing, metabolism, clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment side-by-side.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli ให้ side-by-side management ที่ละเอียดกว่า; Rosen เน้น double-gap differential และเกณฑ์เริ่ม ADH blockade ชัดเจน.

Methanol

Metabolized to formic acid. Think visual symptoms, severe acidosis, basal ganglia injury. Treat with fomepizole plus folinic/folic acid.

Ethylene Glycol

Metabolized to glycolic/oxalic acids. Think renal failure, hypocalcemia, calcium oxalate crystalluria. Treat with fomepizole plus thiamine/pyridoxine/magnesium.

Treatment: Block Metabolism, Correct Acidosis, Dialyze When Severe

1. Resuscitateairway, breathing, circulation, glucose, temperature, co-ingestions.
2. Correct Acidosissodium bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidosis; pH matters for formate toxicity.
3. ADH Blockadefomepizole preferred; ethanol only if fomepizole unavailable.
4. Cofactorsfolinic/folic acid for methanol; thiamine/pyridoxine/magnesium for EG.
5. Hemodialysisfor severe acidosis, visual symptoms, renal failure, instability, high levels.
6. Monitor Reboundcontinue metabolic blockade during/after dialysis until level and acidosis resolve.

Key Points: Alcohols

Double Gap

Early osmolar gap, late anion gap. Normal osmolar gap does not exclude late toxic alcohol.

Methanol

Eyes + formic acid: blurred/snow-field vision, severe acidosis, basal ganglia injury.

Ethylene Glycol

Kidney + crystals: hypocalcemia, calcium oxalate crystals, renal failure.

Isopropanol

Ketosis without acidosis. Supportive care; fomepizole usually not needed.

Withdrawal

Benzodiazepines first-line. CIWA helps when the patient can participate.

Dialysis

Severe acidosis, visual symptoms, renal failure, instability, or high toxic alcohol level: call nephrology early.

Do Not Wait

If suspicion is high, start fomepizole before confirmatory levels return.

Discharge

Ethanol intoxication discharge depends on clinical sobriety, no occult illness/trauma, and safe supervision.

Inline Assessment MCQs

Q1. A 32-year-old man is found unconscious smelling of alcohol. Blood glucose is 44 mg/dL. Besides dextrose, which vitamin must be given BEFORE glucose to prevent acute neurologic deterioration?
  • A. Folate 1 mg IV
  • B. Thiamine 100 mg IV
  • C. Pyridoxine 100 mg IV
  • D. Vitamin C 500 mg IV
Thiamine (vitamin B1) must be given before or with glucose in alcoholic patients to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. Chronic alcohol use depletes thiamine stores; a glucose load without thiamine can exhaust the remaining supply and precipitate acute Wernicke's (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia). Standard practice: thiamine 100 mg IV before glucose.
Q2. A patient with isopropanol ingestion has an elevated osmolar gap but NO anion gap metabolic acidosis. What is the key metabolite of isopropanol and why does anion gap remain normal?
  • A. Formic acid — weak acid that doesn't raise anion gap
  • B. Oxalic acid — buffered by calcium in blood
  • C. Acetone — a ketone that produces no anions
  • D. Acetaldehyde — rapidly cleared by aldehyde dehydrogenase
Isopropanol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetone — a ketone, NOT an organic acid. Acetone does not produce anions, so no anion gap acidosis develops. The osmolar gap is elevated from both isopropanol and acetone (both osmotically active). This distinguishes isopropanol from methanol and ethylene glycol, which produce toxic acid metabolites.

Thai EM Board MCQs

Q1. A 45-year-old man presents with altered mental status, severe anion gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.08, HCO3 6), elevated osmolar gap, and bilateral optic disc hyperemia. He denies alcohol use but admits drinking 'cleaning solvent.' Which antidote should be started IMMEDIATELY?
  • A. Naloxone 2 mg IV
  • B. Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV loading dose
  • C. Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV
  • D. Sodium bicarbonate 3 mEq/kg IV bolus
This presentation — anion gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolar gap, and visual symptoms (optic disc hyperemia → blindness risk) — is classic methanol poisoning. Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) is the first-line antidote: it blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing formation of formaldehyde and formic acid (the toxic metabolites). If fomepizole unavailable, ethanol IV/PO can be used. Hemodialysis is also indicated given the severe acidosis.
Q2. A 28-year-old presents 6 hours after ethylene glycol ingestion (antifreeze). pH 7.15, osmolar gap 38, anion gap 28. Urinalysis shows calcium oxalate crystals. Which finding indicates immediate hemodialysis is required?
  • A. Osmolar gap >20 mOsm/kg alone
  • B. Calcium oxalate crystals in urinalysis alone
  • C. Ethylene glycol level >20 mg/dL
  • D. Severe metabolic acidosis pH <7.25 refractory to treatment
Hemodialysis is indicated for ethylene glycol poisoning with: severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.25 refractory to therapy), serum level >50 mg/dL, renal failure, or deteriorating clinical status despite fomepizole. The presence of significant acidosis, oxalate crystals in urine, and elevated osmolar gap together indicate severe toxicity requiring dialysis in addition to fomepizole. Dialysis removes both ethylene glycol and its toxic metabolites (glycolate, oxalate).
Q3. A patient with chronic alcohol use disorder is brought in with delirium, fever, profuse diaphoresis, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures 48 hours after last drink. Which is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic treatment?
  • A. Lorazepam 2–4 mg IV, repeat every 5–10 min as needed
  • B. Haloperidol 5 mg IV for agitation control
  • C. Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV for seizure prophylaxis
  • D. Propranolol 40 mg PO for autonomic symptoms
Alcohol withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens are treated with benzodiazepines as first-line therapy. GABA-A receptor agonists (benzodiazepines) cross-compensate for the loss of ethanol's GABA enhancement and NMDA antagonism. Symptom-triggered lorazepam (or diazepam) with CIWA-Ar protocol is preferred. Phenobarbital is an alternative for refractory cases. Haloperidol alone is inadequate and may lower seizure threshold.
Q4. In methanol poisoning, the toxic metabolites responsible for metabolic acidosis and blindness are formed via which metabolic pathway?
  • A. Methanol → acetic acid → acetate
  • B. Methanol → methyl peroxide → superoxide
  • C. Methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid (via alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenase)
  • D. Methanol → glycolate → oxalate
Methanol → (alcohol dehydrogenase) → formaldehyde → (aldehyde dehydrogenase) → formic acid. Formic acid is the primary toxic metabolite causing metabolic acidosis. It also inhibits cytochrome oxidase in retinal mitochondria, causing selective retinal toxicity and blindness. Blocking alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole or ethanol prevents this toxic conversion.

Thai EM Board — InTraining Exam MCQs

Q1. A 52-year-old alcoholic presents with confusion, nystagmus, and ataxia after starting IV dextrose for hypoglycemia in the field. No thiamine was given pre-hospital. His current symptoms most likely represent which condition?
  • A. Acute alcohol intoxication with cerebellar degeneration
  • B. Wernicke encephalopathy precipitated by glucose without thiamine
  • C. Hypoglycemic encephalopathy despite glucose administration
  • D. Hepatic encephalopathy from underlying liver disease
Thiamine deficiency in alcoholic patients can be unmasked or precipitated by glucose administration. When glucose is given without thiamine, the remaining depleted thiamine stores are consumed in glucose metabolism, precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. Classic triad: confusion (encephalopathy), oculomotor dysfunction (nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia), ataxia. Treat immediately with IV thiamine 100 mg.

McGraw-Hill Specialty Board Review MCQs

Q1. A patient presents with an osmolar gap of 45 mOsm/kg but a NORMAL anion gap. Serum ketones are positive. Which alcohol ingestion is most consistent with this presentation?
  • A. Ethanol — causes osmolar gap but no ketones
  • B. Isopropanol — metabolized to acetone (ketone, not acid)
  • C. Methanol — formic acid raises anion gap
  • D. Ethylene glycol — oxalic acid raises anion gap
Isopropanol produces an elevated osmolar gap (from both isopropanol and acetone) and ketonemia/ketonuria WITHOUT anion gap acidosis. Acetone is a ketone, not an organic acid, so it does not generate anions. This distinguishes isopropanol from methanol and ethylene glycol, which produce toxic organic acid metabolites causing anion gap metabolic acidosis. Ethanol can elevate osmolar gap slightly but not typically to 45.
Q2. A 38-year-old woman with suspected ethylene glycol ingestion 4 hours ago has pH 7.28, osmolar gap 32, anion gap 22. Which initial intervention is MOST critical to prevent permanent renal failure?
  • A. Sodium bicarbonate infusion to correct acidosis
  • B. Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation to force diuresis
  • C. Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV to block alcohol dehydrogenase
  • D. Calcium gluconate to chelate oxalate ions
Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing conversion of ethylene glycol to glycolaldehyde, glycolate, and oxalate — the metabolites that crystallize in renal tubules causing acute kidney injury. Early administration of fomepizole before significant metabolism occurs is the critical intervention to prevent renal failure. Hemodialysis removes parent compound but fomepizole prevents ongoing toxin production.
Q3. The osmolar gap in methanol poisoning is HIGHEST at which time point relative to ingestion?
  • A. Early — before significant metabolism of methanol has occurred
  • B. Late — when most methanol is converted to formic acid
  • C. 12–24 hours — peak concentration period
  • D. Osmolar gap is constant throughout methanol toxicity
The osmolar gap reflects unmetabolized parent compound (methanol itself). It is highest early after ingestion before metabolism occurs. As alcohol dehydrogenase converts methanol to formaldehyde and formic acid, the osmolar gap decreases while the anion gap increases. A patient presenting late may have a low osmolar gap but high anion gap — falsely reassuring if only osmolar gap is checked. Serial labs are important.
Q4. A 60-year-old man with history of alcohol use disorder is treated with alcohol withdrawal protocol. Despite lorazepam 20 mg over 2 hours, he remains agitated with HR 128, BP 168/100, and tremors. What is the next best step?
  • A. Double the lorazepam dose to 4 mg IV every 5 minutes
  • B. Add haloperidol 10 mg IV for behavioral control
  • C. Start clonidine 0.1 mg PO for autonomic symptoms
  • D. Phenobarbital 10–15 mg/kg IV loading dose
Benzodiazepine-resistant alcohol withdrawal (requiring >40–60 mg diazepam equivalents without adequate control) warrants escalation to phenobarbital. Phenobarbital is a GABA-A agonist with a different binding site than benzodiazepines, providing additive/synergistic effect. It has a long half-life allowing smooth coverage. Propofol with intubation may be needed for extreme refractory cases. Haloperidol alone is insufficient for withdrawal and lowers seizure threshold.

End-of-Chapter Assessment: 20 Questions

Q1. Which of the following best explains why women typically achieve higher blood ethanol levels than men after consuming the same weight-adjusted dose?
  • A. Women have faster hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase activity
  • B. Women have lower gastric alcohol dehydrogenase, reducing first-pass metabolism
  • C. Women have higher body fat which retains ethanol longer
  • D. Women absorb ethanol more rapidly via gastric mucosa
Women have lower levels of gastric alcohol dehydrogenase, resulting in less first-pass metabolism of ethanol in the stomach. This allows more ethanol to reach the systemic circulation. Women also have a lower volume of distribution for ethanol (less body water per kg), contributing further to higher peak levels.
Q2. A 24-year-old man with alcohol intoxication has a serum ethanol of 380 mg/dL but is walking and talking. This is best explained by:
  • A. Laboratory error in ethanol measurement
  • B. Rapid metabolism clearing the drug
  • C. Tolerance from chronic alcohol use — neuroadaptation
  • D. Co-ingestion of stimulant reversing CNS depression
Tolerance is a hallmark of chronic alcohol use. Due to neuroadaptation (upregulation of NMDA receptors, downregulation of GABA-A receptors), chronic users can function at ethanol levels that would cause respiratory depression or coma in naive individuals. Blood ethanol levels correlate poorly with clinical intoxication in tolerant individuals.
Q3. The legal blood alcohol concentration limit for driving in Thailand (and most countries) is closest to:
  • A. 30 mg/dL
  • B. 50 mg/dL
  • C. 80 mg/dL
  • D. 100 mg/dL
Thailand sets the legal limit at 50 mg/dL (equivalent to the standard used in many countries). The US, Canada, and Mexico use 80 mg/dL. Impairment can begin at levels as low as 30–50 mg/dL, especially in non-tolerant individuals, affecting reaction time and judgment.
Q4. A patient with alcohol intoxication and head trauma has a GCS of 10. He smells of alcohol. What is the most important next step?
  • A. Observe until sober then reassess
  • B. Administer thiamine and glucose empirically
  • C. Perform CT head to rule out intracranial injury
  • D. Obtain serum ethanol level to correlate with clinical status
Never attribute altered mental status solely to alcohol, especially with head trauma. GCS of 10 in the setting of head trauma requires CT head to rule out intracranial injury (epidural, subdural hematoma). Alcoholic patients are at higher risk for falls and head trauma. A declining GCS or failure to improve with time should always prompt imaging regardless of ethanol level.
Q5. Isopropanol is unique among the toxic alcohols because it:
  • A. Produces ketonemia/ketonuria but NO anion gap metabolic acidosis
  • B. Causes retinal toxicity and blindness like methanol
  • C. Requires fomepizole as antidote like ethylene glycol
  • D. Produces oxalate crystals in urine
Isopropanol is metabolized to acetone — a ketone, not an organic acid. Therefore it produces ketonemia and ketonuria WITHOUT anion gap metabolic acidosis. All other toxic alcohols that cause serious toxicity (methanol → formic acid, ethylene glycol → oxalic acid) produce anion gap acidosis. This is a key distinguishing feature on exams.
Q6. A patient with methanol poisoning refuses hemodialysis. Current pH is 7.18, methanol level 80 mg/dL, and he is started on fomepizole. The MOST important additional intervention is:
  • A. Add ethanol 10% IV as alternative ADH blocker
  • B. Sodium bicarbonate infusion to correct acidosis and alkalinize urine
  • C. Activated charcoal 50 g PO to reduce absorption
  • D. Leucovorin (folinic acid) to accelerate formate metabolism
Sodium bicarbonate is critical in methanol poisoning for two reasons: (1) it corrects severe metabolic acidosis (formic acid accumulation), and (2) alkalinization promotes urinary excretion of formate and keeps formate in ionized form (cannot cross BBB/retinal cells). Hemodialysis is strongly preferred for pH <7.25 or level >50 mg/dL, but bicarbonate is essential adjunct therapy.
Q7. Calcium oxalate crystals in urine support the diagnosis of which toxic alcohol ingestion?
  • A. Ethanol
  • B. Isopropanol
  • C. Methanol
  • D. Ethylene glycol
Ethylene glycol is metabolized to glycolate → oxalate. Oxalate complexes with calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals, which deposit in renal tubules causing acute tubular necrosis and renal failure. Both monohydrate (envelope shape) and dihydrate (needle/dumbbell shape) forms may be seen. The presence of these crystals in urine is a key diagnostic clue for ethylene glycol poisoning.
Q8. A patient presents with ethylene glycol ingestion. Fomepizole is given. Six hours later, repeat osmolar gap is 8 and anion gap is 26. This suggests:
  • A. Fomepizole is working — osmolar gap down means less ethylene glycol
  • B. Significant metabolism has occurred producing toxic acid metabolites requiring hemodialysis
  • C. The initial diagnosis was incorrect — likely methanol
  • D. Spontaneous resolution — no further treatment needed
The decreasing osmolar gap with increasing anion gap indicates ongoing metabolism of ethylene glycol to toxic organic acid metabolites (glycolate, oxalate) despite fomepizole. While fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, some conversion may already have occurred before treatment, or there is breakthrough metabolism. Hemodialysis is urgently needed to remove both the parent compound and its metabolites.
Q9. A construction worker drinks from a bottle labeled 'windshield washer fluid' at a work site. His wife states he is fine at hour 1 but calls back at hour 8 saying he is confused with blurred vision. What explains this delayed presentation?
  • A. Delayed GI absorption of methanol from food in stomach
  • B. Methanol has direct CNS toxicity only after CNS penetration
  • C. Toxic metabolites (formic acid) accumulate over 4–12 hours — latent period of methanol
  • D. Methanol precipitates ethanol from body stores causing delayed intoxication
Methanol has a 'latent period' of 4–12 hours after ingestion during which the patient may appear only mildly intoxicated (from methanol itself). Symptoms of toxicity (confusion, visual disturbance, metabolic acidosis) are from formic acid, which accumulates as methanol is metabolized over hours. Co-ingestion of ethanol can further delay symptom onset by competitively blocking ADH-mediated methanol metabolism.
Q10. Fomepizole is preferred over ethanol for methanol/ethylene glycol poisoning because:
  • A. Fomepizole is cheaper and more widely available
  • B. Fomepizole is more potent at blocking ADH than ethanol
  • C. Fomepizole avoids CNS depression, hypoglycemia, and need for serum level monitoring
  • D. Fomepizole also accelerates elimination of toxic metabolites
Fomepizole has predictable, easy dosing; does not cause CNS/respiratory depression or hypoglycemia; requires no serum level monitoring; and does not worsen hepatic dysfunction. Ethanol requires careful titration of serum levels (goal 100–150 mg/dL), causes intoxication, and interacts with other medications. Both block alcohol dehydrogenase with similar efficacy, but fomepizole's side effect profile is far superior.
Q11. The CIWA-Ar protocol is used in alcohol withdrawal management to:
  • A. Guide symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing based on withdrawal severity
  • B. Predict which patients will develop delirium tremens
  • C. Determine ethanol blood level without laboratory testing
  • D. Calculate the alcohol content of ingested beverages
The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol-revised (CIWA-Ar) is a validated 10-item scale scoring symptoms (tremor, diaphoresis, anxiety, agitation, perceptual disturbances, seizures, headache, nausea, altered consciousness). It guides symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing — only treating when symptoms exceed threshold — which reduces total benzodiazepine use compared to fixed-interval dosing.
Q12. A patient with severe alcohol withdrawal is refractory to high-dose benzodiazepines (lorazepam 60 mg over 4 hours). The next most appropriate agent is:
  • A. Haloperidol 10 mg IV for agitation
  • B. Phenobarbital 10–15 mg/kg IV loading dose
  • C. Carbamazepine 200 mg PO for seizure prophylaxis
  • D. Clonidine 0.2 mg IV for autonomic symptoms
Benzodiazepine-refractory alcohol withdrawal (requiring very high doses without adequate sedation) warrants phenobarbital. Phenobarbital acts at a different site on the GABA-A receptor from benzodiazepines (barbiturate binding site vs. benzodiazepine site), providing synergistic/additive effect. Loading dose 10–15 mg/kg IV. Propofol infusion is an alternative requiring intubation. Haloperidol is NOT appropriate — it lowers seizure threshold.
Q13. Which classic triad represents Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency?
  • A. Fever, nuchal rigidity, photophobia
  • B. Tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity
  • C. Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia
  • D. Agitation, diaphoresis, seizures
Wernicke encephalopathy presents with the classic triad of: (1) confusion/encephalopathy — global confusion, memory impairment; (2) oculomotor dysfunction — nystagmus, lateral gaze palsy, ophthalmoplegia; (3) ataxia — cerebellar ataxia, gait instability. All three are present together in only ~10% of cases, so empirical thiamine is warranted when any feature is present in a patient at risk. Untreated, can progress to Korsakoff psychosis (permanent).
Q14. A 40-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with ataxia, confusion, and ophthalmoplegia. He is given 100 mg thiamine IV. Forty-eight hours later, despite thiamine, he has profound anterograde amnesia and confabulation. What has occurred?
  • A. Hepatic encephalopathy from underlying cirrhosis
  • B. Alcohol withdrawal delirium developing despite thiamine
  • C. Central pontine myelinolysis from overly rapid correction
  • D. Korsakoff psychosis — irreversible amnestic syndrome following Wernicke's
Korsakoff psychosis (Korsakoff syndrome) is the chronic, largely irreversible amnestic syndrome that can follow untreated or inadequately treated Wernicke encephalopathy. It is characterized by anterograde > retrograde amnesia and confabulation (unconscious fabrication of memories). The mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus are affected. Prompt thiamine treatment of Wernicke encephalopathy is critical to prevent progression to this permanent state.
Q15. A 35-year-old is brought in after drinking antifreeze (ethylene glycol). His initial ethylene glycol level is 180 mg/dL. He is started on fomepizole. What other intervention should be started immediately alongside fomepizole?
  • A. Hemodialysis — level >50 mg/dL is an absolute indication
  • B. Ethanol infusion to maintain level 100–150 mg/dL as backup
  • C. Sodium bicarbonate 3 mEq/kg to prevent calcium oxalate formation
  • D. Calcium gluconate 2 g IV to bind oxalate ions in blood
Hemodialysis is indicated for ethylene glycol poisoning with: (1) level >50 mg/dL, (2) severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.25), (3) renal failure, or (4) clinical deterioration despite fomepizole. With a level of 180 mg/dL, hemodialysis should be initiated immediately to directly remove ethylene glycol before further metabolism can occur, even if fomepizole is blocking ADH. Dialysis also removes already-formed metabolites.
Q16. In assessing a patient with possible toxic alcohol ingestion, the osmolar gap is calculated as (measured osmolality – calculated osmolality). A gap >10–15 mOsm/kg suggests:
  • A. Definitive evidence of toxic alcohol ingestion
  • B. Presence of unmeasured osmoles — consistent with but not diagnostic of toxic alcohol
  • C. Severe metabolic acidosis from anion-forming metabolites
  • D. Impaired renal excretion of serum electrolytes
A normal osmolar gap is <10–15 mOsm/kg. An elevated gap suggests the presence of unmeasured osmotically active substances — the most common being alcohols (ethanol, methanol, isopropanol, ethylene glycol). Other causes include: lactate, acetone, mannitol, DMSO. Critically, a NORMAL osmolar gap does NOT exclude toxic alcohol poisoning — late presentation (after metabolism) may have a low osmolar gap with high anion gap instead.
Q17. A patient who ingested isopropanol (rubbing alcohol) is alert and asking to go home. His vital signs are normal. Labs show osmolar gap 28, ketonemia, but no acidosis. Appropriate disposition is:
  • A. Administer fomepizole to block alcohol dehydrogenase
  • B. Initiate hemodialysis given elevated osmolar gap
  • C. Supportive care and observation — no antidote needed for isopropanol
  • D. Give ethanol infusion to compete with isopropanol for ADH
Isopropanol poisoning management is entirely supportive — there is NO specific antidote and fomepizole/ethanol are NOT indicated (isopropanol's metabolite acetone is not itself toxic). Observation until clinically sober is the correct approach. Hemodialysis is rarely needed (only for very high levels with hemodynamic compromise). The patient should not be discharged while still symptomatic from the CNS depressant effects.
Q18. Formic acid, the toxic metabolite of methanol, causes blindness by which mechanism?
  • A. Direct alkylation of retinal photoreceptor proteins
  • B. Inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase causing histotoxic hypoxia in retinal cells
  • C. Formation of oxalate crystals in retinal vasculature
  • D. Vasospasm of central retinal artery via sympathomimetic mechanism
Formic acid specifically inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) in the mitochondrial electron transport chain of retinal cells. This results in histotoxic hypoxia in the optic nerve and retina — cells cannot utilize oxygen despite adequate delivery. The high metabolic demand of retinal ganglion cells makes them particularly vulnerable. Visual symptoms range from blurred vision to complete blindness and may be irreversible.
Q19. Which of the following is an appropriate use of the CAGE questionnaire in the ED?
  • A. Screening for alcohol use disorder in at-risk patients
  • B. Estimating blood alcohol level from clinical findings
  • C. Predicting severity of alcohol withdrawal
  • D. Determining safe discharge criteria after intoxication
CAGE (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener) is a validated 4-question screening tool for alcohol use disorder (AUD). Two or more positive responses has sensitivity ~70–85% for AUD. It is appropriate for rapid ED screening of at-risk patients. It does NOT diagnose acute intoxication, assess withdrawal risk, or guide treatment — these require clinical assessment and tools like CIWA-Ar.
Q20. A 50-year-old woman with ethylene glycol poisoning is started on fomepizole but fomepizole runs out after one dose. Ethanol IV is not available. Which oral agent can be given to continue blocking alcohol dehydrogenase?
  • A. Naloxone 0.4 mg IV to block any opioid cross-toxicity
  • B. Thiamine 100 mg IV to support cofactor for detoxification
  • C. Oral ethanol (spirits) titrated to serum level 100–150 mg/dL
  • D. Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg/hr to alkalinize blood
When parenteral fomepizole is unavailable, oral ethanol can be used to compete with methanol/ethylene glycol for alcohol dehydrogenase. Goal serum ethanol level is 100–150 mg/dL. Commercial spirits (40% ethanol) can be given orally via NG tube. A common approach: loading dose of 0.8 g/kg ethanol PO, then 0.1–0.15 g/kg/hr maintenance, adjusted based on serum ethanol levels every 2–4 hours.
